title: Strategy and Factory
summary: Swap an algorithm at runtime, and keep the choice of which one in a single place.

steps.title: Patterns are vocabulary
body: A **design pattern** is a named, well-known shape for solving a recurring problem. Knowing them gives you two things:
- a toolbox of designs that have worked many times before
- a shared vocabulary: "make the pricing a strategy" says a lot in four words
They are **not** goals. A pattern earns its place by removing real pain. Adding one "because it is best practice" is the YAGNI trap you met in module 1.

steps.prompt: A teammate wants to add the Visitor pattern to a 40-line script "to make it extensible". What is the best response?
options: Ask which concrete change it would make easier; without one, it is speculative complexity
Agree, patterns are always best practice
Use two patterns to be safe

steps.title: Strategy
body: **Strategy**: define a family of algorithms, put each behind the same interface, and let the caller pick one.
```csharp
interface ISortOrder { IEnumerable<Song> Apply(IEnumerable<Song> songs); }
class ByTitle  : ISortOrder { public IEnumerable<Song> Apply(IEnumerable<Song> s) => s.OrderBy(x => x.Title); }
class ByPlays  : ISortOrder { public IEnumerable<Song> Apply(IEnumerable<Song> s) => s.OrderByDescending(x => x.Plays); }
class Playlist(ISortOrder order) { ... order.Apply(songs) ... }

You used it already for Open/Closed. In C#, a one-method strategy is often just a delegate: `Func<IEnumerable<Song>, IEnumerable<Song>>`. Reach for an interface when the strategy has several methods, state, or a name worth showing.

steps.prompt: When is a `Func<decimal, decimal>` a better choice than an `IPricingStrategy` interface?
options: When the strategy is a single small calculation with no state of its own
When there are many methods per strategy
When strategies need dependency injection of their own services

steps.title: Factory
body: Somewhere, someone must decide *which* strategy to create. Scatter `new Express()` across the code and you are back to the switch problem. A **Factory** puts that decision in one place:
```csharp
static class ShippingFactory
public static IShippingMethod Create(string code) => code switch
"std" => new Standard(),
"exp" => new Express(),
_ => throw new ArgumentException($"unknown shipping '{code}'")
This *is* a switch, and that is fine: it is the **one** place that turns outside input into an object. Everything after it works with `IShippingMethod`.
Overkill check: if you only ever create one type, `new` is the factory.

code: class Loud : IVoice { public string Say(string s) => s.ToUpper() + "!"; }
class Quiet : IVoice { public string Say(string s) => "(" + s + ")"; }
public static IVoice Create(string code) => code == "loud" ? new Loud() : new Quiet();

steps.prompt: Match each problem to the pattern that addresses it.
pairs: Deciding which class to instantiate from input
Only one implementation exists and always will

steps.title: Strategy plus factory
prompt: A text tool supports several transformations. Write:
- `class Upper`, `class Reverse` and `class Snake` (spaces become `_`, all lower case) implementing it
- `static class TransformFactory` with `static ITransform Create(string name)` for `upper`, `reverse` and `snake`; anything else throws `ArgumentException`
starter: string Transform(string name, string s) => name switch
solution: class Upper : ITransform { public string Apply(string s) => s.ToUpper(); }
class Reverse : ITransform { public string Apply(string s) => new string(s.Reverse().ToArray()); }
class Snake : ITransform { public string Apply(string s) => s.ToLower().Replace(' ', '_'); }
public static ITransform Create(string name) => name switch
template: Dojo.Check("upper is an Upper", TransformFactory.Create("upper") is Upper, "Create(\"upper\") should return an Upper");
